facts.claim: Most of this mountain is under the sea. The Hawaiʻi on every postcard is only the top.
facts.notes: USGS FAQ: Mauna Kea 'rises 13,796 feet (4,205 meters) above sea level' and 'extends about 19,700 feet (6,000 meters) below sea level to meet the deep ocean floor'. So about 59% of its height is underwater, before any crustal dent. Pays the title's 'Most of' (packaging promise map): say it means the MOUNTAIN, not land area. No numbers needed in the cold open. Never say Everest, 33,500 or 56,000 in the first 30 s (packaging rule). The USGS FAQ quotes Everest as 29,029 ft (old survey); Ch3 uses 29,032 ft, which is another checker's item.

facts.claim: Every ridge down here is real. Ships mapped most of it with sonar.
facts.notes: HMRG/PacIOOS metadata: 'A 50-m resolution gridded synthesis of all available bathymetry ... including ship-borne multibeam sonar surveys'. It does NOT claim full multibeam coverage, and the far field (ETOPO/GEBCO) is partly satellite-predicted, so 'ships mapped ALL of it' is not safe: keep 'most of it'. OWNER-RULE FLAG: the owner bans 'computed from data' style lines in narration. The sonar clause is a data-provenance line, so the script lead must decide. The safest option is 'Every ridge down here is real.' alone, or drop it. Never put it on screen.

facts.claim: Drop the sea four hundred feet, and three islands become one.
facts.notes: MEASURED (flood-fill on GMRT high-res, about 60 m cells, today's bathymetry). Saddles: Lānaʻi-West Maui about -50 m (-166 ft) near 20.885N 156.758W (ʻAuʻau Channel); Molokaʻi-Lānaʻi about -78 m (-257 ft) near 20.980N 156.950W (Kalohi side); Penguin Bank-West Molokaʻi about -60 m (-197 ft) near 21.105N 157.392W; DIRECT Molokaʻi-West Maui (Pailolo) about -238 m (-781 ft), so the Pailolo Channel STAYS WATER at -400 ft and Molokaʻi joins Maui only through Lānaʻi (matches USGS 2003: 'A permanent embayment separated East Molokaʻi from West Maui by about 700,000 years ago ... these two volcanoes remained connected via Lānaʻi'). Kahoʻolawe-Maui about -159 m (-523 ft) near 20.617N 156.512W, so Kahoʻolawe stays separate at -400 ft; do NOT drain past about -500 ft in this shot or it joins. The three islands actually fuse by about -260 ft, so '400 ft' is safe. State Data Book maximum depths along fixed lines (ʻAuʻau 77 m, Kalohi 165 m, Pailolo 258 m, ʻAlalākeiki 251 m) are consistent; they are maxima, not saddles. VISUAL: the fused island is a horseshoe around a Pailolo bay; Penguin Bank is a big lobe off West Molokaʻi; Oʻahu (Kaiwi saddle about -586 m) and the Big Island (ʻAlenuihāhā saddle about -1,920 m) stay separate. Put the 'No ferry needed' suitcase gag on the ʻAuʻau Channel floor (Lānaʻi-West Maui), never on Pailolo. The HMRG 50 m grid could not be fetched (the PacIOOS TLS chain ends at a root, emSign Root CA - G1, that none of our trust stores hold, and verification was not bypassed). The render team must re-run sill.py on the production grid; the margins (37 m or more) make a different answer unlikely. facts.claim: In the last Ice Age, the sea really was about four hundred feet lower.
facts.notes: NASA: 20,000 years ago 'the average sea level was about 120 meters/400 feet lower than today'. Other estimates run 120-130 m (about 400-425 ft). Always say 'about'. Do not give an exact date; if one is needed, say 'about 20,000 years ago'. USGS 2003 used 'about 18,000 years ago' for the low stand; modern estimates of the Last Glacial Maximum span about 26,000-19,000 years.
facts.editor_note: Script lock: 'That's not a what-if. In the last Ice Age, it really happened.' (s007) and 'The sea rose after the Ice Age and drowned it.' (s013).

facts.claim: That's not a what-if. In the last Ice Age, Maui, Molokaʻi and Lānaʻi were one island.
facts.notes: USGS Volcano Watch (10 Apr 2003, based on Price & Elliott-Fisk 2004, Pacific Science 58:27-45): 'Maui, Lānaʻi, and Molokaʻi were connected intermittently thereafter, most recently about 18,000 years ago.' Do NOT include Kahoʻolawe. Do not say they were 'always' one island (the link was intermittent). Use the ʻokina and kahakō in every label (Molokaʻi, Lānaʻi).

facts.claim: Kahoʻolawe's land link to Maui broke for good long before that, probably 150,000 to 200,000 years ago.
facts.notes: USGS 2003: 'The connection between Kahoʻolawe and Maui disappeared permanently, probably between 200,000 and 150,000 years ago.' Keep 'probably'. Not needed in the narration. It justifies dimming Kahoʻolawe in the -400 ft shot (see C12-03 for the measured saddle).

facts.claim: That flat bank was dry land once. It's the top of a volcano that sank, and coral grew over it.
facts.notes: USGS 2003: 'Penguin Bank originated as a volcano that completed its shield-building stage about 2.2 million years ago', 'Now bearing a thick coral cap and lying in water shallower than 200 m'. GMRT: the bank top sits mostly at about -30 to -60 m, so it was also dry land at the Ice Age low stand (C12-04). Do not say it sank in the last 20,000 years: it went under mainly because the sea rose after the Ice Age, on top of long-term subsidence. Packaging backup title 2 needs both causes named here; see C12-09b.
facts.editor_note: Script lock: the Penguin Bank cake-cut ('the top of a volcano that sank, and coral grew over it') is CUT (it spent Midway's reveal 7 minutes early). s013 says the bank drowned when the sea rose after the Ice Age, per this note.

facts.claim: At its biggest, this joined island was bigger than today's Big Island.
facts.notes: USGS 2003: Maui Nui about 1.2 million years ago 'encompassed about 14,600 square kilometers (5,640 sq mi)' and was 'larger by 50 percent than today's Big Island'. Inconsistency: Hawaiʻi Island is about 10,430 km² (4,028 sq mi), so 14,600 km² is about 40% larger, not 50%. Say 'bigger than today's Big Island'; never '50% bigger'. Not in the Ch1-2 outline; spine item 5 only.
facts.editor_note: Script lock: NOT USED. 'At its biggest, Maui's joined island was bigger than today's Big Island.' is cut: viewers would read it as the -400 ft island (about 5,700 km2, about 55% of the Big Island, measured on GMRT by the red team), and no traced outline of Maui Nui at its largest is in hand. Reserve only with a traced Price & Elliott-Fisk 2004 / USGS 2003 outline: 'Long before the Ice Age, at its biggest, this joined island was bigger than today's Big Island.'

facts.claim: BANNED WORDING: 'All of Hawaii is sinking.'
facts.notes: The absolute 'all' is false in the present tense. Oʻahu 'is thought to be experiencing uplift on the flexural bulge generated by construction of the island of Hawaiʻi' (Toomey et al. 2025, Scientific Reports 15:26462), and emerged reef terraces on Oʻahu, Molokaʻi and Lānaʻi record uplift. The Big Island is the one measured to be sinking now. Use C12-09b.

facts.claim: Part of it drowned when the sea rose after the Ice Age. The rest is slower: these islands sink as they age, and the Big Island is sinking right now, a little every year.
facts.notes: Moore, Ingram, Ludwig & Clague 1996 (JGR, doi 10.1029/95JB03215): 'Island subsidence averages 2.2 mm/yr for the last 47 years' (Hilo tide gauge) and '2.5-2.6 mm/yr for the last 500,000 years' (drowned reefs off west Hawaiʻi). USGS 1992: Hilo sinks at 'nearly one tenth of an inch each year'. If a number is wanted, say 'about a tenth of an inch a year'. Do not say 'a foot a century': USGS 2010 says 'more than 30 cm (a foot) per century' but that includes local Puna fault subsidence, and it conflicts with the 1992 figure of about 10 inches. Spine item 4 ('about 2.5 mm a year') is fine as written. This line also meets the backup-title-2 condition (names both causes).
facts.editor_note: Script lock: both causes stay in Ch1 (backup title 2 condition): s013 (the sea rose) and s014 (the Big Island is sinking right now). 'These islands sink as they age' was cut as abstract.

facts.claim: Those steps are old coral reefs. They grew at the shoreline, and the island sank out from under them.
facts.notes: USGS Volcano Watch (24 Jan 1992): a drowned-reef series off Hawaiʻi, 'the deepest reef being the oldest (about 465,000 years old)' and 'now located 4,380 feet below sea level', the shallowest about 15,000 years old; off Haleakalā 'at depths as great as 6,900 feet'; 'The reefs drowned when the sea level rose as the island was sinking'. The documented series is off WEST (Kohala) Hawaiʻi. Packaging frame 1 looks north from south of the island (lon -155.32, lat 18.42), so draw or label 'drowned reef steps' only where the bathymetry really shows terraces. Below the shelf edge say 'the slope plunges', not 'cliffs' (true cliffs only at landslide headwalls).

facts.claim: Under Hilo, a drill found lava that cooled on dry land, now more than three thousand feet down.
facts.notes: OPTIONAL Ch1 proof that 'it sank'. USGS Volcano Watch (2 Sep 1994): the Hilo hole 'was drilled to 3,464 feet below the surface'; 'All the flows erupted and were emplaced above sea level'; 'Hilo has subsided more than 3,348 feet since the oldest flows erupted'. Say 'more than three thousand feet'. It costs one spoken number, so it competes with the number budget (see C12-14).

facts.claim: Before dawn one morning in 1975, the Big Island's south coast lurched toward the sea.
facts.notes: USGS Circular 740 (Tilling et al. 1976) and Volcano Watch (Nov 2025): mainshock 29 Nov 1975 at 4:48 a.m. HST (the brief's 04:47 is wrong; use 4:48 if ever shown); foreshock M5.7 at 3:36 a.m.; current USGS magnitude 7.7 (originally reported as Richter 7.2; never mix the two); 'the largest Hawaii earthquake of the 20th and 21st centuries'. The south flank 'moved as much as 26 feet (8 m) horizontally'. Do NOT name the 'Hilina Slump' as the source: USGS 2025 puts the primary motion on the décollement fault beneath Kīlauea's south flank, with surface breaks along the Hilina fault system. Safe nouns: 'Kīlauea's south flank', 'the south coast'. No music sting.
facts.editor_note: Script lock: the year is SHOWN (kicker 'NOVEMBER 1975'), not spoken, so 'four hundred' and 'Two' are the only spoken numbers in the first 60-75 s. s016 'One night, campers were asleep at Halapē'.

facts.claim: At Halapē, a beach campsite on that coast, campers were asleep.
facts.notes: VERIFY ITEM CLOSED. Circular 740: the foreshock 'woke ... 32 people camped near the beach at Halape, a coconut palm grove on the southeastern coast'; 'The 32 campers at Halape ... were the first to experience the tsunami.' Volcano Watch 2025: 'Campers at Halapē, on the south coast in Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park'. 'Campers' and the place name are both safe. Spell it Halapē (kahakō). Do NOT say 'Boy Scouts' (only in a magazine first-person account, not USGS/NPS). Do not name the victims (people cap; sources differ). Pin Halapē from GNIS/NPS coordinates; about 25 km west of the epicenter (19°20.1'N, 155°01.4'W). [PD] option: USGS 'Submerged coconut grove at Halapē after 1975 quake', marked Public Domain, no photographer named.
facts.editor_note: Script lock: the [PD] USGS 'Submerged coconut grove at Halapē after 1975 quake' photo runs under s023.

facts.claim: Two people died.
facts.notes: Circular 740: 'the tsunami also caused two deaths'; 'One person was drowned or battered to death ...; another was swept out to sea and is presumed dead. Nineteen people were injured at Halape; seven required hospitalization. Four of ten horses were lost.' Waves 'reached Halape within 30 seconds after the strongest shaking had ended'; people were washed 'into a large, pre-existing crack in the ground, 5-7 m deep and 10 m or more wide'. Solemn, no gag, no sting. NUMBER-BUDGET FLAG: 'four hundred feet' (0:14), '1975' (0:47) and 'Two' (about 1:05) put 3 spoken numbers inside one 60-s window (PLAYBOOK section 4 caps it at 2). Fix by dropping the year ('Before dawn one morning, ...'), or by saying 'Not everyone made it out.' instead of 'Two people died.' (true and respectful), or by moving the beat after 1:14.
facts.editor_note: Script lock: 'Two people died.' kept (speed 0.9, 2.0 s silence after it).

facts.claim: Parts of the shore dropped farther than a basketball hoop is high.
facts.notes: Circular 740: 'The maximum measured subsidence, about 3.5 m, took place in the Halape-Keauhou Landing area'. Volcano Watch 2025: 'subsided by as much as 11.5 feet (3.5 m)'. NBA Rule 1: the ring's upper edge is 10 feet above the floor, so 11.5 ft > 10 ft holds. The brief's 'up to 12 ft (3.7 m)' (Wikipedia) is NOT the measured maximum; use 11.5 ft if a number is ever shown. Kalapana sank nearly 1 m; Punaluʻu rose about 0.1 m. This wording carries no spoken number (good for the budget). VISUAL TRUTH: the coconut palms stayed standing, left in water 'averaging 1.2 m deep and 100-150 m landward of the presubsidence shoreline'; the waves rarely felled the palms but uprooted keawe trees. Do not wash the palms away.
facts.editor_note: Script lock: supports the new s023 'By morning, the palm grove was standing in the sea.' (Circular 740: the palms stayed standing in water averaging 1.2 m deep, 100-150 m landward of the old shoreline; the main shock was at 4:48 a.m., so the grove stood in the sea from before dawn: 'by morning' is safe). The hoop in s020 is a plain silhouette scale marker, not a paper prop.

facts.claim: Then the sea rushed in: a wave nearly fifty feet high, up the coast from the camp.
facts.notes: OPTIONAL. Circular 740: 'The tsunami reached its maximum height of 14.6 m above mean lower low water about 1.5 km east of Halape'; at Halapē it averaged about 9 m in the low ground. Volcano Watch 2025: 'The highest wave reached an estimated 48 feet (14.6 m) above the shoreline east of Halapē'. The brief's '47 ft (14 m)' is off; use 48 ft (14.6 m) or 'nearly fifty feet', and say it was east of the camp, not at it. This is a local tsunami, so do not hype it or link it to mega-tsunamis. It costs a spoken number (see C12-14).

facts.claim: BANNED WORDING: 'That was a few miles of coast.'
facts.notes: Understates the event. Circular 740: faulting 'along a 25-km long zone' of the Hilina fault system, subsidence measured 'along the coastline from Honuapo to Kaimu', and 'the slumping of a large part of Kilauea's south flank'. That is tens of miles, not a few. Use C12-17b.

facts.claim: That was one side of one volcano sliding a few yards. Now picture a whole side of a volcano letting go.
facts.notes: USGS Volcano Watch (5 Jun 1992): 'Moderate to large earthquakes located beneath the south flank of Kīlauea Volcano are commonly caused by seaward sliding'. Circular 740: 'slumping of a large part of Kilauea's south flank'. Horizontal motion up to 26 ft (8 m), which is roughly 8-9 yards, so 'a few yards' is a slight understatement; 'several yards' is also safe. 'A whole side' replaces 'half a volcano' (see C12-21).
facts.editor_note: Script lock: 'All that, from several yards of sliding.' (s024; 'several yards' per the red team: up to 26 ft, about 9 yards; never 'just a few yards'). s025 'Now picture a whole side of a volcano letting go. One did.'

facts.claim: At the Pali Lookout, the wind is usually so strong you can lean on it.
facts.notes: Hawaiʻi DLNR State Parks (Nuʻuanu Pali State Wayside): 'Winds are usually so strong that one can lean against the wall of wind'; the lookout is at 'the brink of pali (cliffs) at 1200 feet elevation in the Koʻolau Range'. Do not quote gust speeds (sources differ: 30-60 mph). GAG PHYSICS FIX: the trade winds blow FROM the northeast, up the windward cliff and into the visitor's face, so a hat blows off BACKWARD (inland, toward Honolulu), not over the edge. The brief's 'hat blows over the edge and down the cliffs' breaks PLAYBOOK_craft section 8 (animation physically true). Options: (a) the hat flies off backward, the man turns, and the camera dives over the edge alone; (b) he holds his hat out over the rail, lets go, and the updraft hands it straight back (single-source lore: coins tossed off the Pali blow back). TASTE: the Pali is where many warriors died in the 1795 Battle of Nuʻuanu. Never stage a figure or object 'falling off the Pali' as the joke, and keep the gag about the wind.

facts.claim: If you've stood here, you may have stood at the edge of a giant break. Rain has worn it back, but these cliffs may trace where a volcano tore apart.
facts.notes: USGS Volcano Watch (14 Jan 2016): 'NUUANU Pali may be the erosional trace of the scarp that marks one of the largest landslides in the world.' USGS hedges with 'may be', so keep a hedge ('may'). The brief's unhedged 'you've stood on the edge of a break' is too strong: the cliff has been eroded back from the original headwall, and some geologists attribute the windward pali mainly to erosion.
facts.editor_note: Script lock: one hedge, kept: s030 'If you've stood here, you've stood at the edge of something huge.' (literal: a 1,200 ft cliff) and s031 'These cliffs may trace where a volcano tore apart.' The rain clause was dropped; 'may' carries the USGS hedge ('may be the erosional trace'). Fact lead to confirm.

facts.claim: Out here lies the debris of one of the largest landslides on Earth.
facts.notes: Moore et al. 1989 (JGR 94(B12):17465, doi 10.1029/JB094iB12p17465): some Hawaiian debris avalanches 'exceed 200 km in length and rank among the largest on Earth'. USGS 2016: 'one of the largest landslides in the world'. Say 'one of the largest', never 'the largest'. The Nuʻuanu tsunami is modelled, not witnessed, so skip it (brief must-fix 3).

facts.claim: DISPUTED WORDING: 'Half of the volcano that built eastern Oʻahu is lying out here.' / chapter card 'Half a Volcano Is Missing'.
facts.notes: 'Half' rests only on secondary sources (Wikipedia: 'The eastern half of the mountain collapsed nearly in half at the caldera'; a 2002 Star-Bulletin piece says 'about 40 percent of the Windward side'). No primary USGS or peer-reviewed text found says 'half'. Primary support is the USGS 1995 line 'The caldera was bisected by the catastrophic collapse of the Nuʻuanu landslide'. A figure of speech on the chapter card is lower risk than a narrated statement. Prefer C12-21b in narration; for the card consider 'A Volcano Split in Two' or 'The Missing Side of Oʻahu'.

facts.claim: The volcano that built eastern Oʻahu split right through its summit. Its whole northeast side is lying out here.
facts.notes: USGS 1995: 'The caldera was bisected by the catastrophic collapse of the Nuʻuanu landslide, which deposited numerous blocks on the sea floor as far as 100 miles northeast of the island.' USGS 2016: Koʻolau 'forms the east side of the island'. USGS I-2809: catastrophic landslides 'carried large parts of some volcanoes as much as 200 km across the sea floor'. Age, if spoken: 'more than a million years ago' (estimates conflict: 1-1.5 Ma on Wikipedia, 1.8-2.1 Ma per Herrero-Bervera et al. 2002 cited by ODP Leg 200, which gives 1.8-2.4 Ma). Never say 'two million years ago'.
facts.editor_note: Script lock: s036-s037 as worded. 'It broke away more than a million years ago' is CUT (abstract age, chronology ran backwards).

facts.claim: The debris runs for more than a hundred miles.
facts.notes: USGS 2016: 'The gigantic NUUANU slide extends across the ocean floor about 200 km (120 mi) northeast from Oʻahu'. ODP Leg 200 IR: 'extends more than 200 km from the island', covering about 23,000 km². USGS 1995: blocks 'as far as 100 miles northeast'. The brief's 'about 125 miles' is a rounded Wikipedia conversion (200 km = 124 mi); use 'more than a hundred miles' (supported by all three) or 'about 120 miles' (USGS 2016). The line on screen must be drawn along the mapped deposit (USGS I-2809), not a guessed path.

facts.claim: DISPUTED WORDING: 'One block is the size of Manhattan.'
facts.notes: USGS 1995 does say 'The largest of these blocks is about the same size as Manhattan Island', but the measurement and the peer-reviewed size both contradict it as an area comparison. MEASURED on GMRT high-res (about 60 m cells): Tuscaloosa Seamount summit -2,691 m at 22.0653N 157.0724W; surrounding floor median about -4,660 m (relief about 1.9-2.0 km); footprint at the -4,100 m contour about 27 x 18 km = about 380 km² (147 sq mi); at -3,600 m about 251 km². Moore et al. 1989: about 30 x 17 km. Manhattan: about 22.7 sq mi (59 km²), 13.4 mi (21.6 km) long, 2.3 mi (3.7 km) wide. So the block is about 4-6x Manhattan's area and longer than Manhattan. A true-size overlay would visibly contradict 'the size of Manhattan'. Use C12-23b.

facts.claim: One block is bigger than Manhattan. Manhattan would fit on it with room to spare.
facts.notes: Supported by the measurement in C12-23a and by USGS 2016 ('one of the blocks ... measures over 29 km (18 mi) long and 1.6 km (1 mi) thick'). OVERLAY: draw Manhattan at true scale from a real polygon (US Census TIGER New York County boundary, public domain), not a hand-drawn shape, laid on the block's summit area at VE 1.0. Optional add-on: 'And it's about a mile thick.' (USGS 2016: 1.6 km (1 mi) thick; GMRT relief about 1.9-2.0 km). That costs one spoken number. Do not say 'six times Manhattan' (the ratio depends on which contour is called the base). Do not name 'Tuscaloosa' (an extra proper noun).
facts.editor_note: Script lock: the Manhattan overlay drapes along the block's LONG axis over the whole block (footprint at about -4,000 m), never on the summit area (above -2,900 m the top is only about 37 km2 and about 6 km long; Manhattan is 21.6 km). The spare room shows mostly in width. No 20-degree turn. Red-team measurement: Manhattan first fits lengthwise at about the -3,100 m contour; at -4,100 m the strip is 26.2 km, area 381 km2.

facts.claim: It's one of dozens of giant slides around these islands.
facts.notes: Moore, Normark & Holcomb 1994 (Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences, doi 10.1146/annurev.ea.22.050194.001003): 'Sixty-eight landslides more than 20 km long are present along a 2200 km segment of the Hawaiian Ridge'. USGS 1992: 'at least 17 major deposits extending away from the islands'. For the 'about 8-10 footprints light up' pullback, trace outlines only from USGS I-2809 'Hawaii's Volcanoes Revealed' (public domain) or Moore et al. 1989, never invented shapes (PLAYBOOK section 4). '68' is fine as a fact but costs a spoken number; 'dozens' carries none.
facts.editor_note: Script lock: 'And it's one of dozens of giant slides along this island chain.' ('along this island chain' per the red team: 68 slides from near Midway to Hawaiʻi; the 8-10 footprints shown are a sample).

facts.claim: They're rare, but they happen.
facts.notes: USGS 1992: 'they occur very rarely, perhaps once every 150,000 years'. USGS 1995: 'only once every several hundred thousand years'. The two USGS frequency figures conflict, so speak NO interval number. No mega-tsunami framing, and no 'overdue' or 'could happen tomorrow' lines.

facts.claim: And Kīlauea's south flank is still creeping toward the sea, a couple of inches a year.
facts.notes: VERIFY ITEM CLOSED, and a rate is now sourced. USGS Volcano Watch (28 Nov 2025): continuous GPS 'recorded the steady seaward motion of south flank at a rate of around 5 cm (2 inches) per year'. USGS 2021: average 'around 8 cm (3 inches) per year' during 1983-2018. The 2018 M6.9 moved it up to about 0.5 m (1.5 ft). USGS I-2809: 'Deformation and seismicity along Kilauea's south flank indicate that slumping is occurring there today.' 'A couple of inches a year' is safe; 'a few inches' is also OK. Drop the rate if the 60-s window already has 2 spoken numbers (Ch2 risk: 'more than a hundred miles' at 2:50, plus the optional 'a mile thick'). Never say it 'will collapse' or is 'overdue'.
facts.editor_note: Script lock: s045 'And it's still creeping toward the sea, a couple of inches a year.' (about 5 cm, 2 in, a year by continuous GPS, USGS 2025). 'Instruments on the flank record that motion nonstop' is CUT (provenance line).

facts.claim: Measured from the sea floor, Mauna Kea is more than thirty-three thousand feet tall. That's taller than Everest.
facts.notes: USGS FAQ (verbatim): 'Mauna Kea Volcano rises 13,796 feet (4,205 meters) above sea level but extends about 19,700 feet (6,000 meters) below sea level to meet the deep ocean floor. Its total height is nearly 33,500 feet (10,211 meters)'. NOAA: 'rises more than 10,210 meters from base to peak'. The two straddle 33,500 ('nearly' vs 'more than'), so: SPOKEN 'more than thirty-three thousand feet'; ON SCREEN the hero counter reads '33,000+ FT' (or 'NEARLY 33,500 FT'), never a bare '33,500 FT' and never '10,000+ M'. Our own ETOPO 2022 check (tools/moat_check.py, moat_map.py) puts the deepest moat floor within 100 km of the summit at about -5,600 m and within 150 km at about -5,760 m, so on our DEM Mauna Kea's relief is about 9,800-10,000 m (32,000-32,800 ft): do NOT drive the counter from the rendered moat floor (it would stop short of 33,500); treat the counter as a label that lands on the word, or start its base line at the USGS base (-6,000 m). Spent fact (17M-view Shorts): keep at 3:55, never in package or first 30 s. Summit elevation differs by source (USGS 13,796 ft; UH 13,803 ft): do not show the above-sea-level figure.
facts.editor_note: Script lock: the Everest staging is fixed per the red team: Everest stands on the sea-level line for s059-s060 ('Above sea level, Everest wins easily' is then true as drawn), then sinks 6,000 m onto the shared USGS base line on 'measured from the sea floor' before the bar climbs. Kicker 'FROM THE SEA FLOOR' is a logged 4-word exception (mandatory qualifier).

facts.claim: Most of this mountain's height is hidden below the waterline.
facts.notes: Pays the title's 'Most of'. Mauna Kea: about 19,700 ft below vs 13,796 ft above sea level (USGS), so about 59% of its height is underwater; our DEM gives about 57%. Mauna Loa: more than 4 km above sea level, submarine flanks about 5 km further down, plus the sea floor depressed another 8 km (USGS FAQ 'Where is the largest active volcano'). Say 'height' or 'mountain', never 'most of Hawaii's land' or 'most of its volume' (volume share not sourced).
facts.editor_note: Script lock: s054 'Today's shoreline is a thin white line, high up its slopes.' ('near the top' was wrong at VE 1.0: the shoreline sits about 57-59% of the way up from the moat floor).

facts.claim: Everest, at the same scale, from the same base line.
facts.notes: Everest 8,848.86 m = 29,032 ft (Nepal-China joint survey, 8 Dec 2020); USGS FAQ still uses the 1954 figure 29,029 ft (8,848 m). Not spoken. VISUAL BUG IN THE BRIEF (fact 3): 'the 5,000 m base cut on the SRTM mesh is used for the base-to-peak comparison' compares Mauna Kea base-to-summit (about 10.2 km) with Everest's upper 3.8 km, which would make Mauna Kea look 2.7x Everest while the narration's claim is 10,211 m vs 8,849 m (1.15x). The USGS/NOAA comparison is against Everest's height ABOVE SEA LEVEL, so in the 3:55 shot and the payoff shot Everest's summit must stand 8,849 m above the shared base line (fill the 0 to about 2,955 m gap under the SRTM mesh with a plain pedestal, or raise the mesh). The payoff line 'Everest reaches roughly halfway' (8,849/17,170 = 52%) is true only with this full-height Everest. VE 1.0 in both shots.

facts.claim: Around the base, the sea floor dips into a deep trench, pushed down by the weight of the islands.
facts.notes: Cause [V]: USGS HVO 'The enormous load (weight) of its volcanoes have caused the underlying ocean crust and lithosphere to sag over a large area'; Volcano Watch 'the lithosphere flexes downward under the increasing weight of the volcanoes'. Depth: Wikipedia 'about 18,045 feet (5,500 meters) deep' citing Rees, Detrick & Coakley 1993 (GSA Bull. 105:189-205); our ETOPO 2022 check agrees: moat floor about -5,350 to -5,600 m within 100 km of the Big Island, deepest -5,790 m north of Maui/Molokai (lon -155.90, lat 21.40); the open floor west of the island is only -4,300 to -4,800 m. If a number is needed say 'about 18,000 feet down' (no on-screen digits; not one of the hero numbers). The arch '200 m' and '14 km radius' are Wikipedia-only [S] (the radius looks wrong; Rees et al. give about 140 km): never narrate them. Call it a trench, moat or trough, NOT a ring (see C3-05).
facts.editor_note: Script lock: s058 'Remember that trench. It's a clue.' and s167 'That trench at its feet is the edge of that dent.' The moat is the unfilled outer part of the flexural depression the load makes (USGS HVO: the crust and lithosphere 'sag over a large area'; Rees et al. 1993 via Wikipedia: the trough is caused by the islands' weight). FACT LEAD TO CONFIRM the word 'edge' before voicing. 'It's the deepest water left around these islands' is CUT (restated s057).

facts.claim: A ring of deep water clings all the way around the island's base.
facts.notes: Brief 3:30 ('A last ring of deep water clings around its base... Remember that ring.') and 10:45 ('Remember that ring of deep water?') are not supported by the data. ETOPO 2022 30-arc-second grid (scratchpad/hawaii_dl/skirt.tif): at a -5,000 m water level the remaining water is a broad crescent on the NE, E, SE and S sides only (west and south-west of the Big Island are dry, floor -4,300 to -4,800 m); at -5,500 m only a strip remains, from north of Molokai/Maui (min -5,790 m) to about 100 km east of Hilo (lon -154.6 to -154.2, lat 19.1-19.8, min -5,589 m). It is never a closed ring around the Big Island, and the Big Island is joined by dry ridge to Maui below about -1,900 m. USE: 'a deep trench curls around the island's east side' / 'Remember that deep trench?'. Render the last water from the real grid at the shot's level (sill/flood-fill per playbook section 4), no sculpted ring. Brief thumbnail-3 note already bans a sculpted ring.

facts.claim: The Big Island is sinking, about a tenth of an inch a year.
facts.notes: USGS HVO: Hilo tide gauge 1947-1983 'the rate of sinking was 2.4 mm (0.09 inch) per year'; general 'a few millimeters (fractions of an inch) per year'. Volcano Watch: 'Hilo... is sinking at a rate of nearly one tenth of an inch each year.' The brief's '2.5 mm a year' (fact 4) comes from Wikipedia citing Volcano World: replace with 2.4 mm / 'nearly a tenth of an inch'. Supports backup title 'What's Holding Hawaii Up? (It's Slowly Sinking)'. Do not apply the rate to the whole chain; it is measured at Hilo.

facts.claim: The Big Island is five volcanoes grown together into one mountain.
facts.notes: USGS: 'From oldest to youngest, they are Kohala, Hualālai, Mauna Kea, Mauna Loa, and Kīlauea' plus a sixth, submarine volcano, Māhukona, 'the oldest of the volcanoes that form the mass of Hawai‘i'. Say 'five volcanoes' only for the ones above sea level; once the drain exposes the whole massif, 'at least five' or just 'one mountain' is safest. STAGING FIX: the brief (3:30) has 'five volcanoes merge into one massif' as the water drops from -4,000 to -5,500 m, but the five are already one island at today's sea level; the deep drain reveals the full body, it does not merge them. Do not say Kamaʻehuakanaloa is part of the island. Labels use ʻokina and kahakō: Kohala, Hualālai, Mauna Kea, Mauna Loa, Kīlauea, Māhukona.

facts.claim: Drain this far and the islands stop being islands: it's one long mountain range.
facts.notes: Own ETOPO 2022 30-arc-second sill check (approximate on a 1 km grid; HMRG 50 m must confirm before any label): Big Island-Maui (Haleakalā) link appears below about -1,900 m; Molokai-Oahu about -580 m; Oahu-Kauai about -3,000 m; Kauai-Niihau about -760 m. So by -4,000 m every main island from Hawaiʻi to Niʻihau is one continuous dry ridge. Never show or say the Big Island standing alone in the -4,000 to -5,500 m shots; frame it as the Big Island end of one ridge. No narration numbers needed.

facts.claim: There's a road almost to the top of this one.
facts.notes: Closes brief VERIFY 20. Center for Maunakea Stewardship brochure: 'Dependable, fully-operable 4WD vehicles with low-range are required for summit travel. The eight-mile summit road rises nearly 5,000 feet and unpaved sections are only wide enough for single-lane traffic.' UH Hilo: Visitor Information Station at 9,200 ft; 'Drivers are required to use 4-wheel drive vehicles above the VIS'; summit access '30min before sunrise; 30min after sunset'. The road reaches the observatories, but the true summit is a cinder cone: 'Puʻuwēkiu, the true summit of Maunakea, is a sensitive area. Casual visitors are asked to enjoy it respectfully from a distance.' So NOT 'you can drive to the top' (the brief's line): use 'drive almost to the top' or 'there's a road nearly to the top'. 2026: state agencies are weighing a toll booth and other changes for the access road; recheck it is open the week of upload. TONE (niche report 4.6, 5.2.5): Mauna Kea's summit and domes are never the punchline; the joke must land on the Everest climber's ordeal (a 4WD on the access road below the summit area is fine), no car or figure on Puʻuwēkiu, no gag about the telescopes. UH writes 'Maunakea' as one word; USGS 'Mauna Kea'; pick one spelling for all labels.

facts.claim: Mauna Loa, the largest active volcano on Earth.
facts.notes: Closes brief VERIFY 18. USGS (three pages, verbatim): 'Hawaii's Mauna Loa is the largest active volcano on our planet'; 'Mauna Loa is the largest active volcano on our planet'; 'Mauna Loa is the largest active volcano on Earth.' Last eruption began 27 Nov 2022. NEVER drop 'active' (no 'largest volcano on Earth / in the world', even though the older Volcano Watch 'How high is Mauna Loa?' says 'Mauna Loa is the largest volcano in the world'): Garcia et al. 2020 (EPSL 542:116296, UH SOEST) found the extinct Pūhāhonu (Gardner Pinnacles, in Papahānaumokuākea) about twice Mauna Loa's volume (148,000 vs 74,000 km3). On-screen label keeps the qualifier: 'LARGEST ACTIVE VOLCANO' (playbook: never drop a qualifier).
facts.editor_note: Script lock: 'It erupted again only a few years ago.' is CUT (date-sensitive; fourth 'It...' fact in a row).

facts.claim: But Mauna Kea isn't the giant here. Its neighbor, Mauna Loa, is a little lower, and far bigger.
facts.notes: USGS: Mauna Loa 'stands not quite as high as Mauna Kea but is much larger in volume'; it 'covers just over half of the Island of Hawaiʻi' and 'by itself amounts to about 85 percent of the area of all the other Hawaiian Islands combined' (optional, numberless version: 'it covers half the island'). 'Giant' must mean bulk, not height (Mauna Kea's summit is higher). Do not give Mauna Loa's volume number (estimates differ by source and method). Hold the 56,000 ft back as planned.
facts.editor_note: Script lock: s069 'It covers about half of this island.' (the red team: 'just over half' rests on a 1% margin; never stage the orange as outweighing the rest). s165 'Under Mauna Loa, the real giant, it's pushed down by miles.' re-anchors the payoff on Mauna Loa, with a MAUNA LOA label held through s169.

facts.claim: And this giant is already sinking.
facts.notes: The brief's 5:15 twist 'And this giant is already dying' is false as worded: Mauna Loa erupted in Nov-Dec 2022 and Kīlauea is in an episodic summit eruption (episode 56 of lava fountaining began 5 Nov 2026, USGS HVO). True and still a twist: 'already sinking' (C3-06) or 'already riding away from the heat that built it' (C4-01). Do not say 'dying', 'dead' or 'finished' about the Big Island.
facts.editor_note: Script lock: s071 'But this giant can't stay. It's already moving.' (never 'dying').

facts.claim: Every island to the northwest was born right here, over the same hot spot. Each one is older than the last.
facts.notes: The brief's 'Every island to the northwest is this same mountain, older' (5:15) and chapter title 'Every Island Is This One, Older' are literally false (each is a different volcano). Safe framing: 'each one shows what the Big Island will become' (USGS: the chain is 'more than 125 volcanoes' that get older to the west-northwest, Kauaʻi 'about 5.0 to 5.5 million years', Midway 'about 28 million years'). Keep the chapter title only as an obvious metaphor or change to 'Every Island Was Once This One'.
facts.editor_note: Script lock: s080 'Every island to the northwest was born right here.'

facts.claim: Deep below, a hot spot melts its way up. The Pacific plate slides northwest over it, a few inches a year, and carries each new volcano away.
facts.notes: USGS Volcano Watch: the Pacific plate carries each volcano 'towards the west-northwest', 'approximately 10 centimeters per year' (Clague & Dalrymple 1987, USGS PP 1350: age progression about 9.2 cm/yr along the Hawaiian chain; UH SOEST gives 5-10 cm/yr by location). If a rate is spoken: 'a few inches a year' (no fingernail comparison: nails grow about 4 cm/yr, so it is wrong). USGS frames the hot spot cautiously ('some scientists think it consists of hotter material'): a glowing plume in the cut-away is fine as a picture, but do not narrate 'a plume from the core' or 'the hot spot has never moved'. If the optional Emperor-bend line is used (Ch5), do not credit the bend only to the plate turning: the hotspot itself drifted during the Emperor stage (Tarduno et al. 2003, Science 301:1064). The candle-under-paper metaphor is fine for the Hawaiian chain.
facts.editor_note: Script lock: the mechanism is told once, inside Ch3 (s071-s075), about 20 s: the candle and paper carry it; the hot-spot glow cut-away is shown once. 'Here's how it works.' and the second explanation after the card are cut.

facts.claim: The Big Island is the baby of the chain: its oldest volcano above water, Kohala, started erupting only about a million years ago.
facts.notes: USGS: 'Kohala began erupting just over 1 million years ago'; the submarine Māhukona is older still and 'last erupted about 300,000 years ago'. Because the submarine Māhukona is older than Kohala, never say 'the whole island is only a million years old' or 'its oldest volcano' without 'above water'. If an age bar shows a value: 'about 1 million years'. Optional line; it costs a spoken number.
facts.editor_note: Script lock: s082 'That makes the Big Island the baby of the islands. A very big baby.' ('islands', not 'chain': Kamaʻehuakanaloa is younger but is not an island). The crash zoom shows the Big Island outweighing all the older islands together (about 10,430 km2 against about 6,400 km2): true.

facts.claim: Give it a million years or so, and it looks like Maui.
facts.notes: USGS: the Maui Nui volcanoes (Lānaʻi, West Maui, Kahoʻolawe, Haleakalā) 'probably occurred between 1.5 and 2 million years ago'; 'The most recent eruption on Haleakalā took place about 400 years ago'. Maui is therefore about 0.5-1.5 million years ahead of the Big Island, so the brief's 'give it a couple of million years' (6:05) overstates: use 'a million years or so', or numberless 'give it time, and it looks like Maui' (saves a spoken number in the 6:05-7:05 window, which already holds 'seven million'). Do not call Maui extinct (Haleakalā erupted about 400 years ago).
facts.editor_note: Script lock: s089 'Give the Big Island time, and it looks like Maui.' The Haleakalā aside is cut.

facts.claim: Older still, Oʻahu, where half a volcano already fell into the sea.
facts.notes: USGS: Waiʻanae 'started growing from the sea floor around 4 million years ago'; Koʻolau's birth 'probably occurred a few hundred thousand years later'. Age bar: about 3-4 million years. Nuʻuanu callback wording is checker #1's (Ch2); keep 'more than a million years ago' for the slide.
facts.editor_note: Script lock: s090 'Older still: Oʻahu, home of Honolulu. Here, a whole side of a volcano slid into the sea.' (Honolulu is named here so the Midway distance drag in s113 stays within the 3-new-proper-nouns cap).

facts.claim: Older still: Kauaʻi, carved into canyons.
facts.notes: USGS sources differ: 'both volcanoes formed about 6 million years ago' (2016 tour) vs 'Kaua`i being about 5.0 to 5.5 million years old'; shield volcanism 'ended by about 4 million years ago, after which, the islands' spectacular canyons and cliffs began to form'. If an age is shown, 'about 5 million years' or '5-6 million'; never '5.1 million' (lab-manual figure, not USGS). No spoken number here (the minute's number is Nihoa's).
facts.editor_note: Script lock: s091 'Its big eruptions ended long ago, and rain has carved it into canyons.' (the red team: Kauaʻi had rejuvenated eruptions until about 150,000 years ago, so not 'its volcanoes went quiet').

facts.claim: Seven million years in, it's a sliver of rock.
facts.notes: Age: K-Ar 7.2 +/- 0.3 Ma (Clague & Dalrymple 1987, USGS Prof. Paper 1350 ch. 1, from Dalrymple et al. 1974); Wikipedia 'formed 7.2 million years ago'. Spoken 'seven million years' or 'about seven million' (this minute's one spoken number). Size: Papahānaumokuākea 'With about 170 acres of land, it is the largest volcanic island in the northwestern chain'; USFWS 'about 1-square km'; cliffs about 900 ft. 'Sliver of rock' is fair; do NOT call it the smallest or say it is 'barely above water' (it is the largest NW volcanic island, with about 900 ft cliffs).
facts.editor_note: Script lock: hero number #4 'ABOUT / 7 MILLION YEARS'; new s095 'Even so, it's the biggest volcanic island left out here.' (Papahānaumokuākea: 'the largest volcanic island in the northwestern chain').

facts.claim: And people lived here. They built homes, farm terraces and shrines on this rock.
facts.notes: Papahānaumokuākea: 'There are 89 identified archaeological sites on Nihoa', including 'residential sites, habitation terraces for dryland agriculture and a plethora of ceremonial complexes'; NPS: Nihoa had 'several long-term habitation sites and agricultural terraces as well as heiau' and 'It is likely that individuals in the past lived there year-round'; USFWS: '35 house terraces, 15 ceremonial structures', burial sites, caves, agricultural terraces. CONFLICTS, so do not narrate: dates (Papahānaumokuākea 'between 1000 and 1700 AD', USFWS 'up until the 13th century', NOAA sheet 'inhabited during the 16th century') -> say 'centuries ago' if a time is needed, never 'around AD 1000'; population (Emory/Cleghorn water estimate 'as many as 100' vs USFWS 'up to 175') -> no number. Nobody lives there now; it is a protected refuge with permit-only access. Draw terraces and house sites only from a published site map, otherwise mark them as approximate or show the real PD photo; no gags here (burials).
facts.editor_note: Script lock: CONFLICT LOGGED (red team): NPS says it is 'likely that individuals ... lived there year-round'; the USFWS Hawaiian Islands refuge page says residents 'likely stayed only a few days or months at a time'. 'Some probably lived here all year round' is therefore CUT. s098 'And they buried their dead here.' (burial sites per USFWS) and s099 'Today, nobody lives here.' The refuge/monument line is cut (admin). If a hedge is ever needed: 'Some may have stayed all year.' (both sources allow it).

facts.claim: At French Frigate Shoals, one rock is all that's left of the volcano: La Pérouse Pinnacle, its last tooth.
facts.notes: USFWS: 'a steep-sided basalt pinnacle that juts out of the water and is the last remnant of the original volcano'. Papahānaumokuākea: 'a basalt rock outcrop rising 122 feet from the lagoon', 'a remnant of the twelve million year old volcano'; named after La Pérouse's 1786 near-wreck. Height by source 120-122 ft (37 m): not spoken (brief plan), on screen at most 'about 120 ft'. The Hawaiian name of French Frigate Shoals is Lalo (NOAA Fisheries): label 'LALO (FRENCH FRIGATE SHOALS)' or say both once. 'Last tooth' must stay local to this volcano (see C4-09).
facts.editor_note: Script lock: s101 'Only one rock of its volcano still stands above the sea. Its last tooth.' (the volcano's bulk is still there below water; the USFWS 'last remnant' means above water). The pinnacle's name is a label only; the French-explorer aside is cut. The place label is 'LALO' only (4-word label fixed).

facts.claim: One more pair of rocks pokes out farther on. After that, no volcanic rock reaches the surface at all.
facts.notes: Papahānaumokuākea: 'In the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands, the last high island in the chain is Gardner Pinnacles' and 'Beyond Gardner, basalt cannot be observed above the surface'. Gardner Pinnacles (Pūhāhonu) lie northwest of French Frigate Shoals. So never call La Pérouse Pinnacle the last volcanic rock in the chain, and the brief's 7:50 bridge ('Keep going, and the last of the volcano sinks out of sight') must either show Gardner as the last rock or stay vague ('Keep going, and the volcanoes sink out of sight one by one'). Optional reserve beat (C4-15).

facts.claim: In 2018, one hurricane washed almost all of East Island away.
facts.notes: Papahānaumokuākea (Nov 2018): 'In early October, Hurricane Walaka ripped through Papahānaumokuākea... as a category three storm' and passed directly over the shoals; 'East Island has been almost completely reclaimed by the ocean', 'a sliver of East remains'. Kane (UH, NOAA HSRP talk 2022): 'East island displaced ~ 100 m, reduced to 5% size'. Civil Beat: an '11-acre spit of sand and gravel'. DO NOT say 'in one night' or 'overnight' (only a news story says so; the monument says 'in early October'), 'erased' or 'gone completely' (5% survived); do not name a storm category (sources say 3 and 4). 'Most of' or 'almost all of' is safe. Before/after shoreline must come from dated imagery (July 2018 vs Oct 2018 per Kane), not a guess.
facts.editor_note: Script lock: the seal beat runs before-to-after once (s102-s108). The storm comes in from the SOUTH-SOUTHWEST moving north-northeast, its eye just west of the atoll and its eastern eyewall across the lagoon (NHC TCR CP012018), per the red team. 'passed right over these shoals' kept (the eyewall did; the monument says 'directly passed over').

facts.claim: Since then, about half of it has washed back.
facts.notes: Kane 2022 (3-year monthly Planet satellite shoreline analysis): 'East island recovered 56% pre-Hurricane size, approx. 12 m/yr' (by July 2021). Civil Beat Nov 2024, UH researcher Kainalu Steward: 'returned to about 60% of the size it was before Walaka'; same article: 'just over half the size it was before the storm but still little more than a sandbar'. So 'about half' or 'more than half' are safe; never '60%' on screen and never 'fully back'. Vegetation has not returned ('The vegetation has yet to return'). The brief's 'It's half grown back since' is acceptable; 'about half of it has come back' is cleaner. Sept 2024: 'a dozen monk seals were basking' and turtles nested there again, which supports the gag's twist.

facts.claim: Hawaiian monk seals used this island to rest and raise pups.
facts.notes: NOAA Fisheries: endangered under the ESA since 1976; 'around 1,600 seals'; 'about 1,200' live in Papahānaumokuākea; Lalo (French Frigate Shoals) is a primary pupping site; 'On land, monk seals haul out to rest, molt, give birth, and nurse'. East Island: NOAA's Littnan via Civil Beat, about 30% of the seals at French Frigate Shoals had pups there [S, number not for narration]. Gag is fine (no deaths implied): most pups of the year were weaned before Walaka (Papahānaumokuākea) and NOAA estimated one mother and pup were on the island; impact unknown, so never show or imply a seal was hurt or lost. The seal model must look like a Hawaiian monk seal (grey-brown, no ear flaps), on the real terrain per the character rules.
facts.editor_note: Script lock: s103 'Endangered Hawaiian monk seals came here to rest and raise pups.'

facts.claim: Hawaiian monk seals are endangered. Only about sixteen hundred are left.
facts.notes: Optional; costs a spoken number, so only if the minute has room. NOAA: 'We estimate the population to be around 1,600 seals'; listed as endangered since 1976. Do not say 'critically endangered' (newspaper phrasing; the ESA listing is 'endangered').
facts.editor_note: Script lock: USED as the stakes line s104 'Only about sixteen hundred are left.' (a spoken number; the 60 s windows pass).

facts.claim: Labels: Hawaiʻi, Mauna Kea (or Maunakea), Mauna Loa, Kīlauea, Hualālai, Kohala, Māhukona, Puʻuwēkiu, Maui, Haleakalā, Oʻahu, Kauaʻi, Niʻihau, Nihoa, Lalo (French Frigate Shoals), La Pérouse Pinnacle, Papahānaumokuākea, Pūhāhonu (Gardner Pinnacles).
facts.notes: Spellings are as the agencies write them. Pronunciations are NOT verified here: the lexicon still needs wehewehe.org (and ideally a Hawaiian speaker) for every name before any narration render (niche report 5.2.4). 'Mauna Kea' (USGS) vs 'Maunakea' (UH): choose one and use it in every label and the description.

facts.claim: Those two little rocks are the tip of Pūhāhonu, a dead volcano scientists measured at about twice the size of Mauna Loa.
facts.notes: RESERVE ONLY (not in the brief). Garcia et al. 2020, EPSL 542:116296: Pūhāhonu volume 148 +/- 29 x 10^3 km3 vs Mauna Loa 74.0 x 10^3 km3; only Gardner Pinnacles show above sea level; name means 'turtle rising for breath'. One peer-reviewed study [V], volume not height. Risk: it competes with the 'Mauna Loa is the giant' setup and the 56,000 ft payoff, so use it only if the payoff wording stays 'largest ACTIVE' and 'tallest from its true base'. If used, say 'about twice the volume' only in the description; the narration can say 'twice the size'. Its existence is the reason C3-10 must keep 'active'.

facts.claim: Under this ring of reef lies a volcano about twenty-eight million years old.
facts.notes: USFWS: 'The atoll, which is 28.7 million years old'. USGS (Dalrymple, Clague & Lanphere 1977): alkalic basalt pebbles from the Midway drill hole show Midway 'erupted lavas of the alkalic suite' 27.0 +/- 0.6 m.y. ago, i.e. late-stage lavas; the shield is a little older. NOAA Ocean Explorer and UH SOEST also say about 28 million years. So 'about 28 million' is safe; never '28.7' or a bare '28 MILLION YEARS' on screen: use 'ABOUT 28 MILLION YEARS' (or a 2-word kicker 'ABOUT' / 'VOLCANO AGE'). The age belongs to the VOLCANO, not the coral: the reef cap is Miocene and younger (USGS PP 680-A), so never 'this reef is 28 million years old'. Hero number #3; it counts as a spoken number.

facts.claim: As the volcano sank, the reef on top kept growing upward. What's left is a ring of reef sitting on a drowned volcano.
facts.notes: USGS HVO: 'As the volcanoes erode and islands subside, they become coral atolls'; 'These coral reefs begin to die as they sink below water depths with enough sunlight'. USGS PP 680-A abstract: the volcanic mound was 'partly truncated by wave action', then 'subsidence began' and clays 'were covered by reef limestones'; submergence 'was interrupted three or more times by emergence'. So do not say it sank 'steadily' or 'nonstop'. Say 'reef' or 'coral reef rock', not pure 'coral' (it is limestone built by corals and other organisms). Do NOT explain why the reef is a RING: the sinking-foundation part is solid, the ring-shape mechanism is debated (see C5-07).

facts.claim: Drills here went down through hundreds of feet of reef rock, and hit the volcano.
facts.notes: USGS PP 680-A (Ladd, Tracey & Gross 1970), verbatim: 'Two holes were drilled during the summer of 1965'; 'The first hole, on Sand Island, entered basalt at a depth of 516 feet' (157 m); the 'Reef hole', drilled from a barge at the north edge of the lagoon, 'entered basalt at a depth of 1,261 feet' (384 m) and went on to 1,654 ft. Depths are from the rig's rotary table, 16.5 ft (Sand Island) and 10.5 ft (Reef) above datum. In the Reef hole about 170 ft of 'reworked volcanic clays' lie on the basalt, so its reef limestone is roughly 1,075 ft. BRIEF FIX (fact 11): 157 m and 384 m are DEPTHS TO BASALT, not 'reef cap thickness' (the Reef-hole figure includes the clays). Cut-away: basalt top about 515 ft under Sand Island, deepening to about 1,250 ft under the north lagoon rim; a thin clay band on the basalt is optional. Safe sizes: 'hundreds of feet' everywhere; 'more than a thousand feet under the lagoon's edge' is also true. If the year is spoken ('In 1965') it counts as a number. Never say this drill 'first proved Darwin right' (that was Enewetak in 1952, C5-06).

facts.claim: Charles Darwin said he worked this out before he had ever seen a true coral reef. He never came here.
facts.notes: Darwin Correspondence Project: Darwin read his coral paper to the Geological Society in May 1837; 'The Structure and Distribution of Coral Reefs' (1842) is his fullest statement; Autobiography pp. 98-9: 'the whole theory was thought out on the west coast of S. America before I had seen a true coral reef.' The DCP notes no South American field note shows the theory 'thought out', so attribute it ('Darwin said...'). PP 680-A: 'Darwin had not visited the area.' Midway itself was first sighted by Captain N.C. Brooks in 1859 (USFWS), 17 years after the book, so Darwin never wrote about Midway: present his idea as a general one about sinking islands. BRIEF FIX (8:15 'Charles Darwin guessed this in 1842'): if a date is used, 'In 1842, Charles Darwin published the idea'; but 1842 + '28 million' + 'June 1942' + 'four' land within about 60 s, which breaks the cap of 2 spoken numbers per 60 s, so prefer the numberless line above. Darwin's theory was about sinking ISLANDS (their foundations), so 'a sinking island' is safer than 'a sunken volcano' when quoting his idea. Show his 1842 woodcut diagram (public domain) with motion, never a portrait.
facts.editor_note: Script lock: one Darwin idea beat (s120), told on our own cut-away, no woodcut. 'He said he worked it out before he'd ever seen a true coral reef' and 'And he never came here' are CUT (idea-history, ep01's failure mode).

facts.claim: Darwin never saw these islands. But on his reef map, he coloured Kure blue: a reef on sinking ground.
facts.notes: OPTIONAL callback for the Kure / Darwin Point beat (9:55). PP 680-A p. A1: Couthouy's description of Kure (then 'Ocean Island') 'led Darwin to color Kure blue on his reef map, thus indicating subsidence; on the same map Darwin colored the larger Hawaiian (Sandwich) Islands red to indicate emergence.' On Darwin's 1842 map blue marks atolls and barrier reefs (sinking areas) and red marks fringing reefs. Use the public-domain scan of Darwin's 1842 map cropped to 5 words or fewer, or tell it on our own map; never fake an 'old map'. Do not claim Midway is on his map (it was unknown until 1859).
facts.editor_note: Script lock: told on OUR map (s141-s142), not the 1842 map crop (unreadable at 390 px; it would also break the 60 s archival spacing).

facts.claim: Darwin didn't live to see it, but in the twentieth century drills finally reached the sunken islands under atolls, just as he had predicted.
facts.notes: Rosen 1982 (BioScience, on Darwin Online): the US Atomic Energy Commission's 1952 hole E-1 at Eniwetak (Enewetak, Marshall Islands) 'first proved Darwin's subsidence beneath an atoll'; 'the celebrated Eniwetak boreholes of 1952' were 'the first atoll drillings to successfully reach volcanic foundations'. DCP: 'test borings in the Marshall Islands confirmed' it, ending a controversy 'until the 1950s'. Darwin died in 1882. Midway's own 1965 holes (C5-03) then reached basalt under the Hawaiian chain's atoll. BRIEF FIX (8:15 'A drill here proved the volcano is down there'): true only as 'a drill here hit the volcano'; never 'the drill here proved Darwin right' or 'first proof'. Optional line, not required.

facts.claim: DISPUTED WORDING: 'Darwin explained why atolls are rings.' / 'That's why it's a ring.'
facts.notes: Brief fact 12 already warns. Even the drilling team (Ladd) said Bikini and Enewetak had undergone 'Darwinian subsidence' but did not appear to have passed through the fringing-reef and barrier-reef stages Darwin postulated (Rosen 1982). Other models (sea-level-driven karst shaping) are debated. Say only that the reef sits on a drowned volcano (C5-02, C5-03).

facts.claim: Midway has the biggest albatross colony on Earth. Most of the world's Laysan albatrosses nest here.
facts.notes: Closes brief VERIFY 17 (colony part). USFWS: Midway 'is home to the largest albatross colony in the world'; 'over 70% of the world's Laysan albatross population' returns to breed. USFWS refuge page: 'the world's largest population of albatrosses'. Smithsonian: '400,000 nesting pairs represent 70 percent of the world's Laysan population'. Bird totals vary by source and year (about 1-3 million birds of all species), so speak no count. Reserve-joke warning: Wisdom (oldest known wild bird) did NOT lay an egg in the 2025/26 season per USFWS via ACAP (Jan 2026), and her 2026/27 status was unknown on 29 Oct 2026, so do not use her as a current fact.

facts.claim: In the air, they're graceful. Landing is another story. On Midway, they're known as gooney birds.
facts.notes: Closes brief VERIFY 17 (nickname part) WITH A FIX. The military-era use is documented: USFWS release of 13 Feb 1955, 'The gooney birds of Midway', on hazards to military aircraft ('black-footed and Laysan albatrosses (gooney birds)'); Audubon: a 'collective nickname for the albatross masses' around Midway's naval air station. Clumsy landings are documented: Island Conservation, 'In the absence of the braking effort of a strong wind, landing birds may occasionally tumble on landing.' But the ORIGIN of the name is not documented: the Honolulu Star-Bulletin (2002) says nobody knows who coined it, sailors used 'goney' for albatrosses in the 19th century, and only magazine prose (NWF 2000) ties it to the landings. So never say 'their landings earned them the nickname' or 'the WWII nickname'. 'The troops here called them gooney birds' is supportable but weaker; prefer the line above. Animate a believable tumble (wings out, forward roll, light wind), on the real terrain at 35-40% frame height.
facts.editor_note: Script lock: s117 'Here, they're known as gooney birds.' over the tumble landing.

facts.claim: In June 1942, the battle that turned the war in the Pacific was fought over this sunken volcano.
facts.notes: USFWS: 'The Battle of Midway was a major turning point in the Pacific Theater during World War II', fought June 4-7, 1942 (Wikipedia: 4-7 June 1942; Smithsonian says 3-7 June, counting the first air attacks). BRIEF FIX (8:45 'the most important spot in the Pacific'): that is opinion; use 'turned the war' / 'a turning point'. Say 'fought over' (Midway was Japan's invasion target and was bombed), not 'fought on': the carrier fight happened at sea, far from the atoll. 'June 1942' counts as a spoken number.
facts.editor_note: Script lock: 'Most of the fighting happened far out at sea' is CUT ('far out' three times in 20 s); the wreck geography carries it.

facts.claim: Weeks before the battle, American codebreakers had Midway send an uncoded radio message: our fresh-water plant has broken down. Then Japan's own coded report passed it along: AF is short of water. AF was Midway.
facts.notes: Closes brief VERIFY 14 WITH FIXES. Agreed by every account found: Station HYPO (idea credited to Jasper Holmes; do not name, people cap) had Midway, ordered over the secure undersea cable so Japan could not hear the order, radio an UNCODED message that its fresh-water equipment had failed; a Japanese intelligence report then said AF was short of water, which Allied codebreakers decrypted, confirming AF = Midway. Smithsonian: the plea went out on May 20, 1942. Wikipedia (Battle of Midway; Joseph Rochefort, citing Layton pp. 421-2 and Holmes, Double-Edged Secrets): 'secure undersea communications cable', 'uncoded' / 'plain-language' request; FRUMEL Melbourne relayed the decrypt with 'This will confirm identity of AF.' Station HYPO site (citing historian Craig Symonds): Midway reported 'that the salt-water evaporators on the base had broken down'; 'Rochefort did it to help convince Washington'. Parker's NSA history (as indexed by search; the NHHC copy returned 503 on 2026-11-08) words it as a message 'in the clear' that the 'water distillation plant had suffered serious damage', followed by an intercepted report that 'AF is short of water'. The breakdown is variously an evaporator, distillation plant or desalination failure, so say 'fresh-water plant'. FIXES: (1) It happened in MAY, so the line must say 'Weeks before the battle' (the brief's 'In June 1942...' followed by the decoy implies June). (2) Not 'we're out of fresh water': the message reported broken equipment and a short supply ('only enough water for two weeks' in one version); 'running short of fresh water' is OK. (3) Say 'confirmed', never 'this is how America found out the target': HYPO already believed AF = Midway, and the ruse was mainly to convince Washington (OP-20-G). (4) Quote marks only around 'AF is short of water', the standard translation; never put Midway's own message in quotes on screen (accounts differ). Re-open the NHHC pages in a browser before showing any verbatim quote. Story humour is fine here (no one has died yet); no gag once the battle starts.
facts.editor_note: Script lock: reported speech, never first person: s128 'So they had Midway radio a message in plain language.' s129 'The bait: its fresh-water plant had broken down.' s130 'Japan bit. A coded Japanese report passed it along.' s131 'AF is short of water.' (the only quote-like line, never captioned in quote marks). The cable detail is dropped (safe per this entry). s126 now says 'intercepted messages' (keeps the 3-new-proper-nouns cap).

facts.claim: Japan lost all four carriers in its strike force. America lost the carrier Yorktown.
facts.notes: 'All four Japanese fleet carriers present at the battle' sank: Akagi, Kaga, Sōryū, Hiryū (plus the heavy cruiser Mikuma). The US lost Yorktown and the destroyer Hammann. Yorktown was crippled on 4 June and sank on 7 June 1942 after torpedoes from the submarine I-168. Never 'Japan lost all its carriers' (it had others elsewhere; USFWS says 'two thirds'). Speak no casualty numbers (about 3,057 Japanese and 307 US dead per Wikipedia; sources vary). Number cap: 'four' is a spoken number; numberless option: 'Japan's whole carrier strike force went down.' NHHC Yorktown photo [PD]: check each catalog entry's credit line (some NHHC images are donated, not Navy-made).
facts.editor_note: Script lock: s135 'Already crippled, it was sunk by a Japanese submarine.' (not 'finished off').

facts.claim: Three of those wrecks have been found: Yorktown, Kaga and Akagi.
facts.notes: Yorktown: found 19 May 1998 by Robert Ballard's National Geographic expedition (MIT News). Kaga: identified 16 Oct 2019 by RV Petrel; Akagi: identified 20 Oct 2019 (Papahānaumokuākea), 'all within Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument'. E/V Nautilus surveyed all three on 8-12 Sept 2023 'in their final resting places' inside the monument. Sōryū and Hiryū: no public report of their discovery was found as of 2026-11-08, but absence of a report is not proof, so do not say 'still lost' or 'never found'; show three markers and say 'three have been found'. Never use OET, NOAA or Vulcan imagery (brief rule); render our own silhouettes.
facts.editor_note: Script lock: 'A research ship has filmed each of them.' is CUT (points at footage we may not use). The three names appear as one text block held 2.5 s or more.

facts.claim: They lie more than three miles down.
facts.notes: Yorktown 'at a depth of 16,650 feet' (5,075 m, 3.15 mi; MIT). Kaga and Akagi 'found 5,400 meters (more than 17,000 feet) below the surface' (Papahānaumokuākea; 3.36 mi). Nautilus 2023: the three surveys took 'a combined 43 hours at depths below 5,000 meters'; the cruise's deepest dive was 5,437 m. AP/Wikipedia give Akagi 5,490 m (18,011 ft), slightly deeper than Nautilus's deepest dive, so give no Akagi-specific depth. 'More than three miles down' and 'about three miles down' are both true for all three. Call the bottom 'the deep ocean floor'; 'flat abyssal plain' is looser than the data (abyssal hills, the flexural arch).
facts.editor_note: Script lock: hero number #6 'MORE THAN / 3 MILES DOWN' in the gauge, soft tick only (war graves); the shot keeps mean luma 70 or more with a lit pool.

facts.claim: Drain it, and you'd find them nowhere near the atoll: far out, more than three miles down, on the deep ocean floor.
facts.notes: No source states the wreck-to-Midway distance, and the discovered wreck coordinates are not published. Our great-circle distances from Sand Island (28.208 N, 177.38 W) to the RECORDED 1942 SINKING POSITIONS: Yorktown (30 deg 35' 59" N, 176 deg 34' 04" W) 277 km / 172 mi, north-northeast; Akagi (30 deg 30' N, 178 deg 40' W) 284 km / 176 mi, northwest; Kaga (30 deg 23' N, 179 deg 17' W) 304 km / 189 mi, northwest. The brief's '170-190 miles' matches. Place the markers at these positions, treat them as approximate (fine at chain scale), and show no coordinates or distance labels on screen. AP's 'hundreds of miles off Midway' is looser than the data; do not use it. Never 'off Midway' or 'around the atoll'. The USFWS '300 miles northeast of Midway' is the US carriers' 'Point Luck', not the wreck site. If a distance is ever spoken: 'nearly two hundred miles away' (only if the 60-s number cap allows).

facts.claim: These are war graves, for American and Japanese sailors alike.
facts.notes: NHHC director Samuel Cox (Nautilus 2023): 'important war graves of both American and Japanese sailors'; NHHC historian Frank Thompson (2019): the wrecks are 'war graves'. Optional line; it justifies the framing rule: music down, no gags, no 'treasure', no gore, respectful silhouettes.

facts.claim: BANNED WORDING: 'Kure, the northernmost atoll (or coral reef) in the world.'
facts.notes: Papahānaumokuākea writes 'Kure Atoll is the northernmost coral reef in the world', and Wikipedia says 'northernmost coral atoll in the world', but Bermuda's coral reefs (BIOS/ASU: 'the northernmost coral reefs of the Atlantic'; John Smith's Bay sits at 32.33 N in NOAA's paleoclimate catalogue) lie well north of Kure (28.4 N), and whether Bermuda counts as an 'atoll' is a matter of definition. A pedant can fault either world superlative. Use C5-17b ('the last atoll in this chain').

facts.claim: This is Kure, the last atoll in the chain. Here the water is so cool that the reef can barely keep up with the sinking. Scientists call this line the Darwin Point. Past it, every island has drowned.
facts.notes: Papahānaumokuākea: Kure 'has reached a latitude where coral growth rates, which decrease in cooler temperatures, are matched by the rate of subsidence'; 'a unique example of an atoll at the critical "Darwin Point"'. Grigg 1982 ('Darwin Point: A threshold for atoll formation', Coral Reefs 1:29-34): the threshold sits at about 29 N at the northern end of the Hawaiian chain; atolls carried past it drowned. USGS Volcano Watch (1993): 'The western-most island in the chain is Kure Island'; beyond it the chain is submerged. BRIEF FIX (9:55 'Past here, coral can't keep up'): at Kure the reef just keeps pace; it is the older islands beyond it that drowned, so say 'barely keeps up' here and 'past it, every island has drowned'. The name honours Darwin (Grigg named it), so the callback is fair without naming a new person. Kure's age ('about 30 million years', Wikipedia via a popular book) has no radiometric date: never speak or show it. Kure: /ˈkʊəriː/ ('KOOR-ee', Wikipedia); Hawaiian name Hōlanikū; both go to the lexicon check.

facts.claim: Beyond Kure, the drowned volcanoes march on across the North Pacific, all the way to Kamchatka, where a deep-sea trench is swallowing them.
facts.notes: Papahānaumokuākea: past Kure the chain continues 'as a chain of submerged platforms that makes a sudden northward bend to become the Emperor Seamounts', which 'extend across the entire North Pacific to the base of the Kamchatka Peninsula in Russia'. Shu et al. 2022 (Nature Communications 13:4467, peer-reviewed): 'across Kamchatka where the Hawaii-Emperor Seamount Chain is being subducted'; Meiji Seamount is the part 'most proximal to Kamchatka'. USGS HVO: the whole chain has 'more than 129 volcanoes' and 'stretches for about 6,100 km (3,800 mi)'; the oldest dated volcano near the northern end is '81 million years' old. BRIEF FIX (fact 13 'The Emperor chain runs about 6,200 km to the Kuril-Kamchatka Trench'): 6,100 km (USGS) is the WHOLE Hawaiian-Emperor chain, not the Emperor part; the far end sits near the junction of the Aleutian and Kuril-Kamchatka trenches, so on screen say only 'TRENCH' or nothing. The age of the bend is disputed (43 Ma in a 1993 USGS column, about 47-50 Ma in Sharp & Clague 2006): show or say no bend age. Globe shot limits apply (4 s).

facts.claim: That's where the Big Island is headed.
facts.notes: BRIEF FIX (10:10 'So that's the Big Island's future'): it is a projection over tens of millions of years, and whether a given island becomes an atoll depends on reef growth against sinking, so frame it as direction, not certainty: 'That's where the Big Island is headed' or 'That's the road the Big Island is on'. USGS: volcanoes 'erode and islands subside, they become coral atolls'; reefs 'begin to die as they sink'.
facts.editor_note: Script lock: moved to right after 'Past it, every island has drowned.' and worded as fate, not place: s146 'That's the road the Big Island is on.' (the red team: today's plate motion does not carry the Big Island to Kamchatka).

facts.claim: Midway lies about thirteen hundred miles northwest of Honolulu.
facts.notes: AP via Hawaiʻi Public Radio: Midway is 'about 1,300 miles (2,090 kilometers) northwest of Honolulu'. Our great-circle check, Honolulu (21.307 N, 157.858 W) to Sand Island (28.208 N, 177.38 W): 2,112 km / 1,312 mi, matching the brief's 2,110 km (1,311 mi). Optional (not in the brief's narration); if used it is a spoken number.
facts.editor_note: Script lock: USED, numberless, as a true-size drag: s113 'It's farther from Honolulu than New York is from Miami.' Editor computation (great circle, mean Earth radius): Honolulu 21.307N 157.858W to Sand Island 28.208N 177.38W = 2,112 km / 1,312 mi; New York City Hall 40.7128N 74.0060W to Miami 25.7617N 80.1918W = 1,758 km / 1,092 mi (matches the brief's unit table). Midway is about 20% farther; the line also holds against the NYC-Miami driving distance (about 1,280 mi).

facts.claim: Just off the Big Island's south coast, about thirty-two hundred feet down, a young volcano is growing. Its name is Kamaʻehuakanaloa.
facts.notes: HVO Volcano Watch (27 Jan 2022): the seamount is 'about 19 miles (30 km) south of the Kīlauea coastline', 'rising to 3,189 ft (975 m) below sea level'; renamed from Lōʻihi in July 2021 by the Hawaiʻi Board on Geographic Names; the name means 'reddish child of Kanaloa'. HVO statements (Aug and Sep 2026): 'Summit Elevation -3199 ft (-975 m)'; 'peak about 1,000 m (3,280 ft) below sea level'. On screen '3,200 FT DOWN' is fine. VISUAL FIX (brief 'a young cone'): Lōʻihi means 'long'; it is an elongated ridge with a summit platform and pit craters, so do not render a neat cone. Place it 30 km south of Kīlauea's coast (HVO coordinates 18 deg 55' 12" N, 155 deg 16' 12" W). Pronunciation goes to the lexicon check.
facts.editor_note: Script lock: '3,200 feet' is no longer spoken or shown (keeps the 90 s before the payoff clear; the gauge marker shows the depth without digits). s151 'Off this coast, under the sea, a young volcano is growing.' (not 'just offshore': it is about 19 miles out). s153 'It means reddish child of Kanaloa.' (respectful, no gag on the name).

facts.claim: BANNED WORDING: 'The next Hawaiian island is already erupting.'
facts.notes: False in the present tense. HVO: 'Kamaʻehuakanaloa's most recent eruption is thought to have been in 1996.' HVO monthly statement of 3 Sep 2026: 'No significant activity was detected... during the past month'; alert level 'UNASSIGNED'. The August 2026 quakes were unrest with no reported eruption. (Kīlauea, on land, IS erupting in episodes, per checker #2; do not mix them up.) Use C6-02b.

facts.claim: It's alive. It last erupted in our lifetime, and this summer it shook the Big Island with a magnitude-five earthquake.
facts.notes: HVO information statement, 11 Aug 2026: 'a magnitude-5.2 earthquake occurred beneath Kamaʻehuakanaloa volcano 26 mi (42 km) east-southeast offshore of Nāʻālehu' at 7 mi (11 km) depth, 'part of an ongoing sequence of earthquakes associated with unrest of Kamaʻehuakanaloa (formerly Lōʻihi) Seamount that started on Sunday, August 9'; felt 'Mostly across the southern and eastern parts of the Island of Hawaiʻi' (intensity IV, light shaking; more than 48 felt reports in the first hour). The 1996 sequence had 'more than 4,000 earthquakes'. Last eruption 'thought to have been in 1996': keep it vague ('in our lifetime') or say 'is thought to have erupted in 1996'; never a flat 'erupted in 1996'. 'This summer' date-stamps the film to 2026 (fine for a Nov 2026 upload; 'in 2026' ages better). Magnitude-five counts as a spoken number; numberless option: 'this summer it set off an earthquake people felt across the island's south'. Do not call it 'strong' (M5.2 is moderate) and do not imply an eruption followed.
facts.editor_note: Script lock: 'It's thought to have erupted within living memory' is CUT (trivia stack). s154 'This summer, it set off an earthquake people felt across the island's south.' (date-sensitive: true for an upload in 2026).

facts.claim: It could become the next Hawaiian island. Opening date: thousands of years from now, at least.
facts.notes: HVO: 'It will be millennia before Kamaʻehuakanaloa emerges' and descendants might one day see it 'finally emerging and forming a new island'. Keep 'could' (brief must-fix 4: 'thousands of years at least'). Older popular estimates of 10,000-100,000 years are not in the current HVO text: do not speak a range. 'COMING SOON' gag is fine (no deaths here).
facts.editor_note: Script lock: 'Opening date: thousands of years from now.' / 'At least.' as two beats (the tag gets its own beat).

facts.claim: We've drained the whole ocean. But we still haven't reached the bottom of this mountain.
facts.notes: USGS Volcano Watch (20 Aug 1998): Mauna Loa's flanks 'continue another 5,000 m (16,400 ft) below sea level to the sea floor', and the volcano 'has depressed the sea floor another 8,000 m (26,000 ft)'. So with all the water gone the true base is still buried about 8 km below the surrounding sea floor. BRIEF FIX (10:45 'Remember that ring of deep water?'): checker #2 (C3-05) found no ring in the data, only a deep trench mostly on the east side; call back 'that deep trench at its feet' instead.
facts.editor_note: Script lock: also supports the cold-open forward promise s010 'Even with every drop gone, we won't hit bottom.' (paid word for word by the Ch6 card and s160).

facts.claim: This mountain is so heavy it has pushed the ocean floor down beneath it, by as much as five miles.
facts.notes: USGS Volcano Watch: 'The massive central portion of the volcano has depressed the sea floor another 8,000 m (26,000 ft)'; 'the Moho was bowed downward by as much as 8 km ... beneath Mauna Loa' (the page's own conversion reads 4.8 mi; 8 km is 4.97 mi). USGS Mauna Loa page: 'the seafloor in turn is depressed by Mauna Loa's great mass another 8 km (26,200 ft)'. HVO: 'As mass increases, the oceanic crust subsides under the weight'. 'By miles' (brief) is safe; 'about five miles' / 'as much as five miles' is safe; keep 'as much as' because 8 km is the maximum under the centre. Cut-away: sag up to 8 km under the summit area, shape schematic (one bowling-ball-on-a-mattress metaphor, 3 s or less, no jargon on screen). 'Dent in the planet' is a fair metaphor for the bent crust and lithosphere; 'dent in Earth's crust' is the literal version.
facts.editor_note: Script lock: the bowling-ball inset is drawn in the cut-away's own look (no separate stylised set).

facts.claim: Measured from its true base, Mauna Loa is about fifty-six thousand feet tall.
facts.notes: USGS Volcano Watch (1998), verbatim: 'Thus, the total relief of Mauna Loa, from its true base to its summit, is about 17,170 m (56,000 ft).' Built from 4,170 m above sea level + 5,000 m down to the sea floor + 8,000 m of depression. USGS Mauna Loa page: 'This makes the volcano's summit about 17 km (55,700 ft) above its base!' 'About 56,000 feet' covers both. ON SCREEN: 'ABOUT 56,000 FT' with the kicker 'FROM ITS TRUE BASE' (never drop either qualifier; craft rule). Always 'Mauna Loa', never 'Mauna Kea' or 'the Big Island' for this number (Mauna Kea's figure is 'more than 33,000 ft from the sea floor', checker #2). Use USGS's phrase 'true base', not 'real base'. Drive the counter from the USGS figures (base line at about -13,000 m under the summit), not from our DEM. Payoff only (87-91% of runtime); never in the first 30 s, the package or a Short hook.
facts.editor_note: Script lock: hero number #7 at about 90% of runtime on both timing models; kicker 'FROM ITS TRUE BASE' is a logged 4-word exception (mandatory qualifier). s168 'Look down. Past the old sea floor. All the way to the bottom of the dent.' with a 0.9 s gap before the payoff take.

facts.claim: Almost twice as tall as Everest.
facts.notes: 17,170 m / 8,849 m = 1.94 (USGS 17 km / 8,849 m = 1.92). 'Almost twice' holds both ways. The comparison uses Everest's height above sea level, which flatters Everest, so it is conservative. Visual: Everest at true scale, VE 1.0, standing on the SAME base line, reaches about halfway (8,849 / 17,170 = 52%). Checker #2's C3-03 fix applies: Everest stands 8,849 m above the shared base line, not cut at a 5,000 m base.

facts.claim: Stand Everest on that same base, and its peak would still be deep underwater.
facts.notes: OPTIONAL, our own arithmetic from the USGS figures: the true base lies about 5,000 + 8,000 = 13,000 m below sea level under the summit area, so an 8,849-m Everest standing there would top out about 4,150 m (13,600 ft, about 2.6 mi) below the sea surface. It stays true for any depression greater than about 3,850 m, so it survives the 'as much as' hedge. Numberless, vivid and on the same frame as the payoff; do not stack a spoken number on it. Show the old sea level line in the same shot.

facts.claim: BANNED WORDING: 'Every beach and every postcard of Hawaii is the very top of a mountain almost twice as tall as Everest, slowly sinking into the dent it made in the planet.'
facts.notes: Overclaim. The 56,000-ft figure is Mauna Loa's (USGS); Waikīkī and every other postcard beach on Oʻahu, Maui and Kauaʻi sit on other volcanoes, and Oʻahu is thought to be rising on the flexural bulge, not sinking (checker #1, C12-09a). 'Every' fails. Use C6-09b.

facts.claim: Every postcard of the Big Island shows only the very top of a giant: a mountain almost twice as tall as Everest, slowly sinking into the dent it pressed into the planet.
facts.notes: Scope it to the Big Island, whose biggest volcano is Mauna Loa (USGS: it covers just over half the island, checker #2 C3-11); 'a giant' / 'a mountain' then means Mauna Loa's massif. 'Slowly sinking' is checker #2's C3-06 (Hilo about 2.4 mm a year). 'The dent it pressed into the planet' = C6-05. Must be over the refill shot that returns to the frame-1 composition. One sentence, 29 words: if the 15-word sentence rule is enforced, split: 'Every postcard of the Big Island shows only the top of a giant. A mountain almost twice as tall as Everest, slowly sinking into the dent it made.'

facts.claim: This fall, the sea arch at Hōlei, on the Big Island's coast, collapsed into the ocean. The waves had carved it out of lava over centuries.
facts.notes: REAL. NPS Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park release, 1 Oct 2026: the 90-ft arch was seen standing on Wednesday 23 Sept and had collapsed by Sunday night 27 Sept 2026; 'the exact moment of collapse is unknown' and it may have fallen while the park was closed for Tropical Storm Nolo. NPS place page: 'about 90 ft. (27.4 meters) high', 'cut into the cliff of an ancient lava flow from about 550 years ago due to "differential erosion"', 'sculpted by the sea', at the end of Chain of Craters Road. Earlier damage: 2018 Kīlauea earthquakes, new cracks in January 2020, and later a chunk knocked off by Tropical Storm Darby surf (sources disagree on that year: do not mention). FIXES: the niche report's 'collapsed on Oct 2, 2026' is wrong (Oct 1 is the NPS confirmation, the collapse was 23-27 Sept; CNN reported it Oct 2). NPS states no cause for the collapse, so never 'the storm destroyed it' or 'the sinking island broke it'; do not tie it to subsidence at all (erosion is a separate process). 'The waves carved it' is supported by 'sculpted by the sea'. Placement: Ch6 before the payoff only (no new topic after the payoff). Numbers: '90-foot' and '550 years' are optional and would break the cap near the 3,200-ft and 56,000-ft beats; keep it numberless. Show it as a before/after on our own terrain or a PD NPS photo (check the credit line: NPS photos are usually public domain, but some are by volunteers). Pronunciation 'Hōlei' to the lexicon.
